Short of time? Read the key takeaways.
🧭 Decide what you want to improve by changing your job. Three things you might want to improve include:
Those are different goals, and the same career move may affect them differently.

🧩 Interestingness is a weak guide to job satisfaction. Career quizzes tend to focus on finding jobs that fit your interests, but it's important to consider other (stronger) predictors of satisfaction such as autonomy, connection with colleagues, and whether the work feels meaningful.
🔍 Diagnose your dissatisfaction before deciding to leave. Some feelings are likely to follow you from job to job, but others won't. Consider whether reshaping your current role could help.

💰 A bigger salary does not guarantee a happier working life. Higher income is more strongly associated with life satisfaction than with job satisfaction or moment-to-moment happiness, so weigh a raise against your other priorities.

🧪 Learn what a job feels like before committing to it. Imagination is often a bad guide, and it is subject to biases. It can be better to ask people doing the work about their typical day, and test potential career changes through small projects, courses, volunteering, or temporary roles.

🌤️ A fading honeymoon period does not mean a job change was a mistake. Even if you do change job and experience a boost in happiness/satisfaction, that boost is likely to fade with time. That being said, temporary improvements can still make a move worthwhile.

Suppose you’re burnt out or unhappy and wondering whether changing your job would make things better. You imagine a few possibilities and you take a quiz to help you discover possible new paths. Then you sit there, looking at the options you’ve been given, and you think: “Would any of these actually make me happier?”

Career quizzes can be helpful starting points or sources of ideas, but they probably can’t answer the question you’re asking on their own. Quizzes typically measure how well a job fits your interests, and research finds that fit has only a small correlation with satisfaction (ρ = 0.19).
Group 1: 100 people in jobs that fit their interests well, and
Group 2: 100 people in jobs that fit poorly.

Those research findings are equivalent to roughly 60 people in the first group being more satisfied than average, compared with 40 people in the second group. That’s better than a coin flip, but not by much. Studies indicate that a job that fits your interests is somewhat more strongly linked to job performance than job satisfaction (closer to 66 against 34). So quizzes are probably slightly better at telling you where you’d do well than where you’d be happy.

So, what does predict satisfaction? How can you improve your chances that a career change would make you happier? The answer involves some features of you and some features of the job. Unfortunately, people tend to be worse at predicting their own feelings than you might think, but by understanding the important features discussed in this article, you’ll be better equipped to better predict how different career options might affect you.
Do you want happiness or satisfaction?
If you’re considering a job change, it’s worth reflecting on why. What is it you want to improve? It could be:
Job satisfaction (i.e., how happy you are with your job overall)
Moment-to-moment happiness (i.e., how good you feel at any given time – in and outside your job)
Life satisfaction (i.e., how happy you are with your life overall)

(Of course, you might also be focused on specific tangible outcomes – like higher income or adequate health insurance – we’ll touch on the impacts of money on happiness, but otherwise those aren’t the focus of this article).

If you want to change jobs because your current one is getting you down, then job satisfaction is likely to be something you care a lot about. But maybe you’re more motivated by a desire to find time for things outside of work that will bring you more moment-to-moment happiness, or maybe you’re after a status increase that you believe will increase your life satisfaction. We discuss all three of these different goals below, but we focus most on job satisfaction.
How much of it is you?

Some amount of your job satisfaction comes from you (rather than the job) and therefore travels with you, from job to job. Studies of identical twins who were raised apart suggest that around 30% of the differences in job satisfaction between people are linked to genetic factors (also here). And nearly half of that genetic link seems to run through your general emotional tendency (how readily you feel upbeat or low), and about a quarter through personality traits such as how outgoing or anxious you are. Sometimes when someone seems really happy at their job, the truth is they’d be happy with almost any job – that’s just their disposition.

That doesn’t mean your job satisfaction is fully determined by things outside of your control (like your genetics or how you feel about your last job), but it does mean that if your job is wearing you down, it’s worth asking yourself: “How much of my feeling is down to the job, and how similar would I feel anywhere?” If you’re confident that a significant portion of your dissatisfaction really is down to the job, that’ll help you with what to look for in the next one.
Decades of empirical research on this topic points to a variety of features associated with greater satisfaction or well-being at work. These include:

In workplace studies, “autonomy” refers to how much control you have over what you do and how you do it. In a systematic review of nearly 200 studies, this was the job feature most strongly linked to how satisfying people found the work itself. A more recent review of 99 studies corroborated the existence of an association between autonomy and job satisfaction, moment-to-moment happiness, and life satisfaction. That review also found that other features such as competence and “relatedness” (feeling connected to others) are also positively associated with those outcomes. These ideas (competence, autonomy, and relatedness) are part of what's known as “Self-Determination Theory,” which says that humans are naturally inclined toward personal growth and thriving when these three basic psychological needs are met.
Here’s another useful term for thinking about your work: “job crafting.” It means actively reshaping your job (insofar as you are able) by doing things like:
changing the people you work with or how you interact with them, or
adjusting how you see the purpose of the work.

A meta-analysis of 20 studies (including 6,599 workers) found that people who engaged in more job crafting tended to be more satisfied (r = 0.29). Since this is only correlational data, it’s always possible that more job crafting doesn’t cause more satisfaction – maybe being more satisfied causes more job crafting, or a third factor causes both increased satisfaction and increased job crafting (such as autonomy). However, these findings suggest that before you leave a job, it’s worth reflecting on what you could change where you are and whether such changes might improve things for you, before you decide to move on.
Feeling that your work makes a difference
Meta-analyses also find relationships between job/life satisfaction and the significance or meaningfulness of work. For example:
“Task significance” (i.e., how much someone views their job as affecting the lives of others) was found to be correlated with job satisfaction (r = 0.41)

“Meaningful work” (i.e., which the worker believes “accomplishes significant, valuable, or worthwhile goals”) was found to be correlated with job satisfaction (r = 0.74) and life satisfaction (r = 0.47)

These findings are, of course, also just correlational (not the result of randomized experiments), but they suggest that if you’re struggling with job/life satisfaction and you’re thinking about changing jobs, you might want to consider where you will find the most significant or meaningful work.

An increase in wages can make a job look much more attractive, but how much should you factor it into your decision? Research indicates that income has a different relationship with each of the three goals we mentioned above (job satisfaction, moment-to-moment happiness, and life satisfaction). Let’s talk about each one.

Job satisfaction: Higher wages do tend to come with a slight increase in job satisfaction, but the increase is small: a meta-analysis of 61 studies found a correlation of 0.15. And studies that do find an increase after a job change also find that the boost in satisfaction tends to taper off over time. If job satisfaction is your main motivation, then wages are probably not the best thing to prioritize.
Clearer Thinking has written about the relationships between income and moment-to-moment happiness / life satisfaction in more detail elsewhere, so here’s a shorter summary:

Moment-to-moment happiness: For most people, a raise of a fixed percentage gives about the same boost in moment-to-moment happiness, regardless of income. So, someone who doubles their $30,000 wage on average is expected to report the same increase in happiness as someone who doubles their $200,000 wage. The exception, as discovered by Nobel Prize winner Daniel Kahneman in his adversarial collaboration with Matthew Killingsworth and Barbara Mellers, is the least happy 20% of people. For those people, they found that extra income stops increasing happiness above an annual income of about $90,000. This suggests that, if you’re deeply unhappy and earning over $90,000, more money is unlikely to be the fix you’re looking for.

But something critical that is easy to miss (even if you read the relevant papers) is that the effect sizes for the association between income and moment-to-moment happiness are very small across the board, as the chart below shows:

People reporting on the effects of income on happiness often emphasize that money does seem to buy happiness (for the happiest 80% of people), but they tend to leave out the fact that the increases in happiness are very small. Perhaps a more appropriate headline would be, “People with vastly different levels of income have surprisingly similar levels of moment-to-moment happiness.” Why this is the case is genuinely a mystery. Presumably, people with more money are able to have more control of their moment-to-moment experiences, for instance, by avoiding taking on jobs they despise, or by hiring people to do things that they don't like to do. Yet on average they experience very little increased moment-to-moment well-being.
Life satisfaction: Things are a bit different for life satisfaction, which seems much more sensitive to income, as this chart illustrates:
Source: “Subjective Well-Being and Income: Is There Any Evidence of Satiation?”, Betsey Stevenson and Justin Wolfers, NBER Working Paper 18992, April 2013. Reformatted in the Economist

Making more money is associated with moderately greater life satisfaction. Looking at US data, every doubling in income is associated with an average increase of 0.6 on a 10 point life satisfaction scale, regardless of your starting income (compared with a 0.1 increase in moment-to-moment happiness on a 10 point scale).

However, a three-year randomized trial found that cash payments to low-income adults initially boosted life satisfaction but the boost faded in the second and third years of receiving payments. This suggests that the life satisfaction you get from a higher paying job may not be permanent. For more discussion of this, check out this Clearer Thinking podcast episode featuring Eva Vivalt – an economics researcher working on some of these issues.
So, what does money buy, in terms of happiness? Higher wages are associated with:
A small increase in job satisfaction, which tapers off
A modest increase in life satisfaction, which can also differ by country
A small increase in moment-to-moment happiness (which reaches a limit for the unhappiest 20% of people)
This suggests that the extent to which money should play a role in your career decisions depends on what you’re aiming for.
Why can’t you imagine new jobs accurately?

Researchers have observed that people tend to overestimate how strongly a change will make them feel and how long it will make them feel that way. That’s one reason why a new job (like any change) can feel less good than you might have expected, despite your confidence that it was the right move.

Part of the explanation for this is a cognitive bias known as the “isolation effect.” This occurs when you’re making a choice, and you ignore features shared by different options to instead focus on features that distinguish them more sharply (even though details about the shared features might be much more relevant to your decision). This is illustrated well by a study of college students, in which they were asked to predict how happy they’d be in their assigned houses. The students focused on physical features of the houses that were very different across the options, and gave less weight to the social features that were more similar but which had a greater impact on their happiness.

When you’re thinking about a job change, it’s worth keeping that cognitive bias in mind: you might be tempted to focus on things that seem very different about your different job options (e.g., title, salary, office), because these are obvious differentiators of the options, but your happiness may well be much more affected by the fine details of things that the options have in common.

On top of that, less obvious differentiators like what is involved in the day-to-day work probably have a bigger impact on how you’ll actually feel. If you want to really hone in on what could be involved in different job options, a useful resource is O*NET. It’s a free U.S. database that breaks jobs down into their everyday tasks and activities. It also has a Career Changers Matrix that takes your current or most recent job and suggests jobs you could move into without much retraining.

Another reason why imagination isn’t the best guide to career decisions is “impact bias”, which is the human tendency to overestimate how bad things will feel and for how long. For example, in one study, people expecting a breakup predicted that they would experience far more distress than they actually did (though they did judge their longer-term recovery fairly well, on average). Findings like this provide some comfort if you’re nervous about switching jobs: the difficult aspects of the change are often easier to get through than you might expect.
So, what’s better than using your imagination?
Instead of just relying on your own imagination to tell you how a different job would compare to your current one, here are some things you can do:
(1) Seek out insights from someone already doing the job.

An interesting illustration of this can be seen in a study that gave students either (a) facts about an experience (speed dating or peer-evaluation), for them to simulate how it would make them feel, or (b) details about how the experience had made another student feel. Then the students were given the experiences and asked how they felt. They tended to think that the facts would be more useful for predicting their feelings, but it turns out that the details about how other people felt were much more helpful (reducing error by half or more).

If you’re considering a job change and you want to know how it will affect you, these kinds of findings suggest that reaching out to chat to someone already doing the job is likely to be more informative than you might think! It can be especially informative to ask about their day to day experience. For instance, you might ask them to walk you through a typical day, hour by hour. What time do they arrive at the office? What do they usually spend that first hour doing? And so on. And you can get even more insight by asking them what it feels like during those hours – is their type of job stressful, exciting, or something else entirely?

(2) Particularly when you’re considering a massive change, you may want to try testing out the new job before committing to it completely. Here’s a list of things you can do that gradually increase in commitment:
Reading or watching informational content about the job
Talking to people who currently do the job
Take a short course that gives you relevant training
Start a relevant project or volunteer with a relevant organization
Take a secondment, contract, or internship with a relevant organization

By raising your commitment gradually, you give yourself the ability to learn without giving much up. If you get a few steps in and realize that the job isn’t for you, then it’s more likely you’ve not had to burn any bridges or leave better opportunities behind. All too often, people spend years preparing for a new career (such as law or medicine) while having almost no clue what it’s like actually working in those professions – they are enticed by the concept of those professions, rather than what they are truly like. While some people really enjoy those jobs, others find themselves deeply disappointed when they finally start working in them.
(3) Seek out career support. A meta-analysis looking at the effectiveness of career choice programs found that a few key features of career support were most helpful:
Individualized feedback on goals and plans
Help gathering information about specific career opportunities
Hearing from people who’ve made the move you’re considering
Attention to building wider support for your career (outside of the career support programs being studied)
It’s normal for satisfaction to fade

Even in cases where changing jobs is the right call for you, you should know that there is evidence that job satisfaction tends to follow a honeymoon-hangover pattern whereby it jumps up when you start a new job but then gradually slides back over the following year (more evidence can be seen here). Perhaps unsurprisingly, the biggest jumps in satisfaction tend to be seen in people who most disliked the job they were doing before.

Another factor that affects how much of a jump in satisfaction you’re likely to experience (and how long it takes to wear off) appears to be how you leave. Studies have found that people who choose to quit experience a larger jump than those who leave by mutual agreement or are dismissed. And among people who moved from the private sector into the public sector, the boost to satisfaction appears to stay higher for longer on average.

It’s common for boosts in satisfaction (or happiness) to be temporary and for people to gradually head back towards a baseline level – this phenomenon is sometimes called “the hedonic treadmill,” though how long it takes varies a lot from person to person. The key point here is just that gradually returning to a baseline level of satisfaction is normal and doesn’t mean that a change was a mistake. Periods of satisfaction or happiness above your baseline can deeply enrich your life, and the fact that something passes doesn't mean you can’t find it worthwhile. (Not to sound too existential, but: After all, everything passes eventually.) But knowing that these boosts are likely to be temporary lets you make more informed decisions.
Is it too late to switch?

In this penultimate section, let’s talk briefly to just the folks who might be later in their careers. Something that makes switching jobs intimidating is that it can feel like starting over – particularly if it involves a career change. If you’re in your 40s, 50s, or older, this can come with a lot of worry. It can help to know that this kind of late change is more common than you might think. A study that followed US workers over 50 for 14 years (between 1992 and 2006) found that:
43% had changed employers by their late sixties
63% of those who changed employers also changed occupations
91% of people who changed reported enjoying their new job, compared with 79% who reported enjoying their old one

That being said, studies do also find that age discrimination is not uncommon in hiring practices (also here and here). Unfortunately, the evidence for discrimination is stronger than the evidence for any strategies to combat it (and of course, it shouldn’t really be your responsibility to mitigate that discrimination). Nevertheless, here are some practical tips that you can try:

Use your contacts to get introductions and information. You can tell people you’ve already established relationships with (e.g., former colleagues, clients) that you’re considering a change and ask who could give you advice, introductions, or even recommend you for something.

If possible, talk to your current employer about whether there’s any opportunity to move internally or reshape your current role. This is the cheapest option, and it lets you skip external recruitment processes.

If you have the time and financial flexibility, consider how you might build a track record on the side by taking on consulting, freelance, or portfolio work to build and demonstrate your skills. You can also consider volunteering, or a trustee role in your new field while you keep your current job.

No study or quiz can answer that question definitively for your specific circumstances, but the empirical research discussed above gives some guidance on how you can make the decision for yourself. Here’s some of that guidance distilled into a short list of steps:

Identify your goal. Do you want more job satisfaction, more moment-to-moment happiness, or more life satisfaction (or do you need to hit a specific concrete target, like making a certain salary)? Empirical research says slightly different things about each.

Diagnose the problem. Try to pinpoint things that are making you dissatisfied or unhappy and categorize them into things that are (a) features of the job (e.g., autonomy, the people), vs. (b) things that might follow you anywhere. Then reflect on whether there are ways you could craft your current job to include more of the features you want, to make sure you don’t miss an opportunity to make your current work better.

Find out about your options. When you find possibilities for new jobs, consider:What it would involve day-to-day (and even hour-to-hour) and whether those things address the needs you’ve diagnosed, or improve on your day-to-day experience.Other people’s experience, by talking to those who are doing the job now, their reactions likely predict yours better than your imagination does!

Consider whether it makes sense to commit gradually (particularly for larger changes). Starting with small, low-risk experiments means that you can keep your options open and learn about them without losing out.
Seek out career support. Consider getting support from someone who has already made the change, getting a career coach, or joining groups or programs for career change.
